overview: Ceratosaurus nasicornis was a medium-large Late Jurassic theropod of the Morrison Formation, about six metres long, recognised by a prominent nasal horn, smaller paired brow horns, and a unique row of small osteoderms along the dorsal midline. It coexisted with the larger and more common Allosaurus.

Ceratosaurus belongs to Ceratosauria — a lineage that diverged from the main tetanuran theropods early in the Jurassic. Its comparatively longer teeth and possible association with fish-bearing deposits have led to suggestions of a partially aquatic hunting strategy, though this remains debated.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Named by O. C. Marsh in 1884 from a well-preserved skull and much of the skeleton found during the Bone Wars at Garden Park, Colorado. The dorsal osteoderms — small keeled bones along the back midline — are unique among large theropods and may have functioned in display. At least two species are recognised.

articles.title: Anatomy and comparison with Allosaurus
articles.body: Ceratosaurus had four-fingered hands (Allosaurus had three) and proportionally longer teeth. Biomechanical work suggests its skull was less optimised for high bite force than that of Allosaurus but that its more flexible tail may have aided aquatic locomotion. The nasal horn is formed by fused nasals.

articles.title: Niche partitioning with Allosaurus
articles.body: Allosaurus was far more common at most Morrison sites. Ceratosaurus may have hunted nearer water margins, taking fish and crocodylians as well as dinosaurian prey — a different ecological role within the same predator guild. Isotopic and bone pathology evidence offers partial support for this hypothesis.

record.description: Ceratosaurus nasicornis was a horned ceratosaurian theropod from the Morrison Formation of western North America. The holotype preserves a skull and much of the skeleton; additional specimens improve coverage, while several proposed species and referrals remain disputed.
facts: The midline nasal horn core and paired orbital rugosities are directly preserved.
A midline row of small osteoderms is associated with the holotype, but their complete arrangement is unknown.

presentation.heroLead: A horned, blade-toothed predator of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, known from one remarkably complete skeleton and a scatter of later finds that still fuel debate over how many species it contained.

animalParagraphs: Ceratosaurus was a medium-sized meat-eating dinosaur that lived alongside Allosaurus and Torvosaurus on the floodplains of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation. The name-bearing skeleton from Garden Park, Colorado, belonged to an animal about five to six metres long; isolated bones from Utah and Colorado suggest that some individuals grew larger, although no complete large adult is known.

It is instantly recognisable from a blade-like horn core on the nasal bones and a pair of low ridges above the eyes, all of which are directly preserved. Its teeth were unusually long for the size of the skull, its arms were short with a four-fingered hand, and its tail was deep and flexible. A row of small bony plates ran along the back, a feature otherwise almost unknown among theropods.

Ceratosaurus belongs to Ceratosauria, a lineage of predators that split early from the tetanuran line leading to birds. It was less common than Allosaurus in the same rocks, and its long teeth and deep tail have prompted suggestions, still untested, that it hunted different prey or in different settings.
animalHighlights: A midline nasal horn core and paired brow ridges are preserved on the holotype skull.
Very long, blade-like teeth in a comparatively short, deep skull.
A row of small osteoderms along the back, associated with the holotype skeleton.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Recurved, serrated teeth and a deep skull indicate a predatory diet. No bite-marked prey or gut contents are directly attributed to Ceratosaurus.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs, short forelimbs and a fused pelvis in the holotype leave no doubt about two-legged walking; speed is not measured.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The holotype is a subadult or small adult. Larger jaws and limb bones from Utah and Colorado imply bigger individuals, but their exact length is estimated.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The bony horn core and dorsal osteoderms are real; the keratin covering, skin texture and colour are inferred.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Garden Park, near Cañon City, Fremont County, Colorado, USA

locality.name: Garden Park (Felch Quarry 1)
locality.note: Morrison Formation. Further material comes from Dry Mesa Quarry and Fruita in Colorado and the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry in Utah; a Portuguese record from the Lourinhã Formation is debated.

presentation.classificationSummary: Ceratosaurus is the name-giving member of Ceratosauria, an early-branching group of theropods distinct from the allosaurs and tyrannosaurs. Within Ceratosauria it is usually placed close to Genyodectes and outside the abelisauroid radiation.

related.reason: Compare with the far more common large predator of the same Morrison Formation floodplains.
Compare with the largest Morrison theropod, a megalosauroid found in the same quarries.
Compare with a later, horned ceratosaur from the Cretaceous of South America.

questions.title: How many species were there?
questions.copy: Ceratosaurus magnicornis and C. dentisulcatus were named from Fruita and the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry, but several studies treat their differences as growth or individual variation within C. nasicornis.

questions.title: Did it live outside North America?
questions.copy: A partial skeleton from the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal has been referred to Ceratosaurus, but the referral rests on limited overlapping material and is not universally accepted.

questions.title: What was the horn for?
questions.copy: The nasal horn is too thin to have been an effective weapon. Display is the usual interpretation, but there is no direct evidence of how it was used or whether it differed between sexes.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure C. nasicornis material is Kimmeridgian-Tithonian in the Morrison Formation.

specimens.note: Associated skull and skeleton from Garden Park, Colorado, described by Marsh in 1884 and monographed by Gilmore in 1920.

panel.headline: One largely complete skeleton with skull, plus scattered later finds.
panel.standfirst: Ceratosaurus rests on the Garden Park holotype, an associated skeleton with a nearly complete skull collected in 1883–1884. Later specimens from Colorado, Utah and possibly Portugal add larger bones and partial skulls, but none is as complete as the first.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: The holotype covers most skeletal regions, with additional partial skulls and postcrania from several later specimens. The forelimb and the end of the tail are less well represented, and no other individual approaches the holotype in completeness.

metrics.label: Known remains
metrics.value: Skull and most of the skeleton

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype USNM 4735 preserves a crushed but nearly complete skull with lower jaws, most of the vertebral column, the pelvis, hindlimbs and parts of the forelimbs, together with a row of small osteoderms. Referred specimens add partial skulls, jaws, vertebrae and limb bones.
knownRemains.note: The holotype skull was distorted during burial, so some proportions in mounted reconstructions are corrected estimates. Larger referred specimens are incomplete, which is why the maximum size of the genus is uncertain.

media.title: Gilmore's 1920 skeletal reconstruction of the holotype
media.alt: Skeletal reconstruction of the Ceratosaurus nasicornis holotype from Gilmore's 1920 monograph, with preserved bones and osteoderm positions indicated
media.caption: Charles Gilmore's 1920 reconstruction of holotype USNM 4735, showing the elements known at the time and the positions of the dorsal osteoderms. Gilmore's upright pose reflects the era; the bone inventory is what matters here.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Nearly complete holotype skull with nasal horn core, brow ridges and lower jaws; partial skulls and maxillae in later specimens.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and most caudal vertebrae of the holotype, with ribs and chevrons; the tail tip is incomplete.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete pelvis and hindlimbs of the holotype; the shoulder girdle and forelimb are only partly preserved, with a four-fingered hand.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: A row of small osteoderms associated with the holotype; no skin impressions, colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: USNM 4735 · holotype
specimenCards.description: An associated skull and skeleton collected by Marshall Felch at Garden Park and described by Marsh in 1884, then monographed by Gilmore in 1920. It remains the most complete Ceratosaurus known and is on display at the Smithsonian.
specimenCards.meta: Garden Park, Colorado · Morrison Formation · National Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: Later Colorado and Utah specimens
specimenCards.description: Partial skulls and skeletons from Fruita, Colorado, and the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry, Utah, were named as C. magnicornis and C. dentisulcatus in 2000. Dry Mesa Quarry material and a Portuguese partial skeleton are also referred to the genus.
specimenCards.meta: Morrison Formation · Lourinhã Formation (debated) · species status unresolved

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: A near-complete skull with horn core, most of one skeleton, dorsal osteoderms, and partial skulls and bones from several other individuals.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A medium-sized ceratosaurian predator that coexisted with, and was rarer than, Allosaurus; its horn is usually read as a display structure.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether the named species are distinct, the maximum adult size, the full osteoderm arrangement, the horn sheath, and any details of hunting behaviour.
